cards.text: Psalm 95 opens with an invitation, and the psalmist did NOT bring his indoor voice. Come, he tells God's people, let us sing for joy to the LORD and shout to the Rock of our salvation. No humming politely in the back row, friend, we are SHOUTING.

cards.question: The psalmist calls God's people to enter the LORD's presence with ___ and to make a joyful noise to Him in song.
All this singing and shouting has a reason, and verse 3 gives it. What does the psalmist call the LORD?

answers.text: A great King above all gods
A mighty warrior at the gate
A wise judge over the nations

cards.text: Then the psalmist shows how big this King is: the depths of the earth are in His hand, the mountain peaks belong to Him, and the sea is His. Meanwhile I spent years in ONE junk drawer, and I didn't even own THAT.

cards.question: The psalmist says the sea belongs to the LORD because He ___ it, and His hands formed the dry land too.

cards.text: Then comes a second invitation, O come, and now the psalmist calls the LORD our Maker, the One whose hands formed all that sea and land.

cards.question: The psalm started with shouting and singing. In verse 6, how does the psalmist call God's people to come before the LORD their Maker?
In verse 7, the psalmist says the LORD is our God and then paints a picture of His people. What are they?
The picture of sheep in the LORD's pasture means God's people are on their own to find food and safety.

cards.text: Then, halfway through verse 7, the whole mood flips with "Today, if you hear His voice," and a warning. It's like a group chat full of party emojis, until somebody types, "Hey. Can we talk?"

cards.question: The warning starts with Today, if you hear His voice. What does it tell God's people not to do?

cards.text: The warning points back to Meribah and Massah in the wilderness. In Exodus 17, verses 1 through 7, the Israelites had no water, so they quarreled with Moses, Israel's leader, and tested the LORD, asking whether He was among them or not.
Now the voice in the psalm changes. God Himself speaks, and He says that there, your fathers tested and tried Him.

cards.question: God says the fathers tested and tried Him at Massah. What makes it even worse?

answers.text: They had made Him a promise

cards.text: That's like watching me stamp a thousand perfect cookies, then turning around and asking, "Okay, but can he STAMP though?" Now God tells how He felt about that generation, and for how long.

cards.question: God says He was angry with that generation for ___ years, and He said they are a people whose hearts go ___.
God says that generation had known His ways.

cards.text: So God swore an oath in His anger about that generation. Friend, no jokes on this one. This is the most serious line in the whole psalm.

cards.question: What did God swear about that generation?

answers.text: They will never enter His rest
They will never see His face
They will never build His house

findings.problem: The question itself says the people "make a joyful noise to Him in song," and card 1 just said "we are SHOUTING." Together these rule out the wrong answer "silence" before the baker picks.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: "Verse 3 gives it" points to a verse number, which makes this read like a test question instead of Papa Dorin pausing mid-psalm.

rule.text: Ask from inside the passage, the way a storyteller pauses to let the listener lean in. The question comes out of the moment Papa Dorin just set up.

findings.problem: "His hands formed the dry land too" ties the blank to "formed," so "made" is the only option that fits the word "too." The wrong answers "calmed" and "divided" are ruled out by the question's own wording.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The joke puts Papa Dorin in God's place and makes the Israelites who tested God the butt of the joke ("Okay, but can he STAMP though?"). It laughs at the people in the passage instead of at himself.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself. Humor about people in Bible stories laughs with their human situation, never at them.

findings.problem: The second blank ("hearts go ___") asks the baker to guess the psalm's exact wording, "astray" versus "cold." After the warning about hardened hearts in verse 8, "cold" is just as reasonable, so the baker can't reason their way to the right word.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop. There are 6 multiple choice cards, 3 fill in the blank cards and 2 true or false cards.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
